pharmacology.mechanism: A rosmarinic-acid-enriched Perilla extract reduced neutrophil and eosinophil infiltration in nasal lavage of people with seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis [46]; the molecular target was not defined.

compound.absorption_bioavailability: In six healthy men given a Perilla extract, rosmarinic acid, its methylated form and ferulic acid appeared in plasma mostly as glucuronide/sulfate conjugates, and only 6.3 ± 2.2 % of the dose was recovered in urine [45]. Treat it as a poorly bioavailable polyphenol that is extensively conjugated and partly broken down to smaller phenolic acids.

evidence.claim: A rosmarinic-acid-enriched extract improved some symptoms of mild seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.
evidence.test_article_detail: Perilla frutescens extract enriched for rosmarinic acid (not a greenhouse species)
evidence.outcome_summary: Higher responder rates for nasal itching and eye symptoms vs placebo over 21 days; no adverse events.
evidence.note: Rosmarinic acid is the named active, but the test article is a whole extract; not transferable to herb teas.

processing_stability.note: Presence at up to 6 % of dried lemon balm leaf [8] and in hydroethanolic extracts [21] shows it survives drying and extraction; heat and solubility values not sourced.

compound.teaching_note: Named after rosemary, but lemon balm is the richer source (up to 6 % of dried leaf) [8]; comparing the Lamiaceae rows side by side shows how shared records make the family comparable.
gaps: Rosemary value is Duke leaf 'max 3500 ppm' whereas Ph. Eur. requires ≥3 % total hydroxycinnamic derivatives; reconcile.
Oregano row has no database record (paper only).
Topical HSV evidence belongs to lemon balm extract (taxa file), not to isolated RA.
